source.title: How Visual Representations Map to Language Feature Space in Multimodal LLMs
source.authors: Constantin Venhoff; Ashkan Khakzar; Sonia Joseph; Philip Torr; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure values are not given numerically in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a trained linear adapter can map visual representations into a frozen language model's feature space, using SAE reconstruction, sparsity, and feature-description alignment rather than the original sources' measures. It does not test convergence with model scale or performance.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the paper's own layer-wise measures of visual-to-language-feature mapping. The benchmark scores in Table 1 are not representation-alignment results and are not included. The paper's adapter is deliberately trained to map visual features; these findings address mapping with that adapter, not spontaneous convergence among independently trained models.
record.test_reason: It trains a linear map from a frozen CLIP ViT into a frozen Gemma-2-2b-it and probes, with the LLM's own SAEs, whether mapped visual tokens are represented by native LLM features. This bears on V4, whether one model's representations map onto another's by a simple linear map with little loss. It uses a different method (SAE reconstruction, sparsity, feature-description match) from the originals. The map is trained, as V4 permits, and is not an induced behaviour. There is no scale sweep, so V1 and V2 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors also stress a 'fundamental misalignment' between ViT outputs and early LLM layers. They question whether adapter-based architectures optimally support cross-modal learning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a trained linear adapter between a frozen CLIP vision encoder and a frozen Gemma LLM, then measures SAE reconstruction, sparsity, and semantic feature-description alignment. It does not measure representational similarity between independently trained models or sweep model scale.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer is associated with a marked change: the reported measures converge around layer 18, whereas earlier layers remain misaligned.
record.problems: The analysis uses one vision encoder, one LLM, and one trained adapter, so it does not establish a general trend across models. Figure values are not numerically available in the supplied text, and no uncertainty estimates are stated. The adapter is trained specifically to map visual inputs into the LLM space.
record.rows_left_out: Intermediate per-layer points from Figures 1 and 2 are not separately recorded; the text summarizes the transition as occurring around layer 18, and the plotted values are figure-only.

untested.parts: No sweep over model scale or capability, and no comparison of independently trained models.
No test of whether vision–language alignment grows as either model improves; one ViT and one LLM only.
Only one ViT→LLM pair and one linear adapter. No stitching, relative representations, unpaired mapping, or language-to-language mapping.
No test of whether features recur across models.
No comparison of alternative similarity metrics, or of in- versus out-of-distribution inputs.
No test of plateaus or of whether shared data explains alignment.

missing.what: Task performance of the linearly mapped model (e.g. MME perception 920.19, POPE F1 75.58), roughly comparable to LLaVA-v1-7B. This is functional evidence on how lossy the linear map is.

record.verdict_notes: Single model pair, no uncertainty estimates, and all key results are figure-only. The convergence layer and its full-alignment interpretation come from the authors' text, not from numbers. The semantic match measure depends on the GPT-4o judge and the feature-filtering thresholds.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model scale or capability, and no comparison of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No test of whether alignment between vision and language models rises as both models improve; the language model and vision encoder are frozen, and only the adapter is trained.
No comparison across random initializations or shared feature subspaces among same-architecture networks.

Tests a trained linear adapter from one frozen vision encoder into one frozen LLM and SAE-based evidence of feature mapping. Does not test stitching, relative representations, unpaired-data mapping, or mappings among independently trained language models.
Feature descriptions are checked for matching image concepts, but the study does not test whether the same features or circuits recur across different models.
Uses several measures, but does not compare alternative similarity metrics, metric settings, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs to test metric or data dependence.
Does not test whether alignment plateaus across models or whether shared training data or objectives explain alignment.

relationships.condition: CLIP ViT-L/14 → frozen Gemma-2-2b-it via a linear adapter; mid-to-late LLM layers (around layer 18 of 26)
relationships.reason: Authors report that SAE reconstruction error and sparsity fall, and that the feature-description match rate rises, converging around layer 18. They read this as visual tokens fully mapped onto LLM features (r2, r4, r6). The evidence is figure-only and rests on the authors' statements.
relationships.display_finding: SAE reconstruction error and sparsity decreased while feature-description matches increased, converging around layer 18 of 26.

relationships.condition: Same model; early LLM layers (before about layer 18)
relationships.reason: The linear map targets the LLM's input space, yet visual tokens remain misaligned with the LLM's SAE features in early layers. The mapping is not native to the layers it feeds directly into (r1, r3, r5).
relationships.display_finding: Despite projection into the LLM input space, visual tokens remained misaligned with its SAE features before about layer 18.
